summary: This Wikipedia article describes hindsight bias, the tendency to perceive past events as more predictable than they were, also called the knew-it-all-along phenomenon or creeping determinism. It traces the concept's history from Fischhoff's 1970s research through later experiments, and covers factors such as outcome valence and severity, surprise, personality, age, auditory effects, and cognitive models (SARA, RAFT, CMT). The excerpt ends partway through a discussion of memory distortions, including Cavillo's 2013 study and Kane's 2010 study of paranormal beliefs.
one_line: Hindsight bias is the tendency to see past events as more predictable than they were, with its history, factors, and cognitive models.
key_facts: Hindsight bias is also known as the knew-it-all-along phenomenon or creeping determinism.
Hindsight bias is the common tendency for people to perceive past events as having been more predictable than they were.
Hindsight bias is a significant source of overconfidence regarding an individual's ability to predict the outcomes of future events.
In 1973, Baruch Fischhoff attended a seminar where Paul E. Meehl stated that clinicians often overestimate their ability to have foreseen the outcome of a particular case.
Beyth and Fischhoff devised the first experiment directly testing the hindsight bias, using judgments about US President Richard Nixon's upcoming visit to Beijing and Moscow.
The Beyth and Fischhoff paper was titled "I knew it would happen," which may have contributed to the phrase "knew-it-all-along phenomenon".
In 1975, Fischhoff developed a method, then called the "creeping determinism hypothesis", that gives participants a short story with four possible outcomes, one of which they are told is true.
Hindsight bias is more likely to occur when the outcome of an event is negative rather than positive.
In malpractice lawsuits, the more severe a negative outcome is, the more dramatic the juror's hindsight bias.
In 1996, LaBine proposed a scenario in which a therapist did not warn a threatened individual; participants in the serious injuries condition were more likely to rate the therapist as negligent.
Surprise influences how the mind reconstructs pre-outcome predictions, and surprise biases the sense-making process by enhancing recall of surprise-congruent information.

The three cognitive models of hindsight bias reviewed are SARA (Selective Activation and Reconstructive Anchoring), RAFT (reconstruction after feedback with take the best), and CMT (causal model theory).
The SARA model was created by Rüdiger Pohl and associates.
Cavillo (2013) found that the hindsight bias index was greater among participants asked to respond more rapidly than among those allowed more time.
In a study by Kane (2010), students in a skepticism class falsely remembered recalling a much lower level of belief in paranormal phenomena at the start of the course than they had initially rated.
